macro: The Fed held its target range at 3.50%-3.75% in July with a rare three-way dissent toward a hike, and markets have since priced rising odds of a 25bp increase at the September 15-16 FOMC meeting. The Fed's preferred gauge, core PCE, held at 3.3% year-over-year in June while headline PCE cooled to 3.7% from May's 4.1%, the first monthly deceleration in six years, though a rebound in oil prices tied to stalled Iran talks and fresh tariffs on Canada, Brazil, and roughly 60 other trading partners threatens to reverse that relief. This week's calendar is inflation-heavy: July CPI lands Wednesday, PPI and jobless claims Thursday, and retail sales alongside the preliminary University of Michigan sentiment read on Friday. The single most important date to watch is Wednesday's CPI print, which will shape whether the Fed leans toward a September hike or a hold.

mortgage_rate: The 30-year fixed mortgage rate averaged 6.69% in Freddie Mac's survey for the week of August 6, up from 6.66% the prior week and an 11-month high. Higher borrowing costs continue to weigh on affordability even as home-price growth persists, a combination that has kept existing-home sales on a declining trend.
personal_finance_deep_dive: The New York Fed's Q1 2026 Household Debt and Credit Report put the credit card delinquency rate at 13.1%, the highest reading in 16 years, even as total card balances eased slightly to $1.25 trillion. The pattern points to a widening gap between households that carry revolving balances and those that don't: card debt is compounding faster than incomes for a meaningful subset of borrowers, while transitions into early-stage delinquency have held roughly steady near 8.6% annually, suggesting the stress is concentrated rather than broadening sharply. The New York Fed's Q2 2026 report, covering the months since, was scheduled for release today, which will show whether that 16-year high is a peak or the start of a longer climb.
wealth_building_deep_dive: U.S.-listed ETFs pulled in more than $1 trillion in the first half of 2026, the earliest the industry has ever crossed that threshold, with State Street projecting $2.3 trillion for the full year. Low-cost, broad-market funds captured roughly half of that money, and active ETFs took another 39%, showing the flows are concentrated in simple, diversified building blocks rather than speculative niches. For a reader building a portfolio this week, the practical takeaway is that a low-cost core index holding — the same category absorbing the bulk of institutional and retail flows alike — remains the most-used foundation, with any satellite positions sized as a minority of the total.
